claim: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) crops have been widely planted.
source: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) crops have been widely planted and the effects of Bt-crops on populations of the target and non-target insect pests have been well studied.
evidence: This is a general statement about the widespread adoption of Bt crops, supported by the broader scientific literature context.

claim: The effects of Bt-crops on populations of target and non-target insect pests have been well studied.

claim: Infection of Helicoverpa armigera with HaDV2 is associated with enhanced growth.
source: Here, we use laboratory and field data to show that infection of Helicoverpa armigera with a densovirus (HaDV2) is associated with its enhanced growth and tolerance to Bt-cotton.
evidence: This claim is supported by laboratory and field data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Infection of Helicoverpa armigera with HaDV2 is associated with tolerance to Bt-cotton.
source: Here, we use laboratory and field data to show that infection of Helicoverpa armigera with a densovirus (HaDV2) is associated with its enhanced growth and tolerance to Bt-cotton.
evidence: This claim is supported by laboratory and field data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Field monitoring showed a much higher incidence of cotton bollworm infection with HaDV2 in regions cultivated with Bt-cotton than in regions without it.
source: Moreover, field monitoring showed a much higher incidence of cotton bollworm infection with HaDV2 in regions cultivated with Bt-cotton than in regions without it, with the rate of densovirus infection increasing with increasing use of Bt-cotton.
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data collected across multiple regions.

claim: The rate of densovirus infection increases with increasing use of Bt-cotton.
source: Moreover, field monitoring showed a much higher incidence of cotton bollworm infection with HaDV2 in regions cultivated with Bt-cotton than in regions without it, with the rate of densovirus infection increasing with increasing use of Bt-cotton.
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data showing correlation between Bt-cotton use and infection rates.

claim: RNA-seq suggested tolerance to both baculovirus and Cry1Ac were enhanced via immune-related pathways.

evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Exposure to Bt-crops has selected for beneficial interactions between the target pest and a mutualistic microorganism that enhances its performance on Bt-crops under field conditions.
source: These findings suggest that exposure to Bt-crops has selected for beneficial interactions between the target pest and a mutualistic microorganism that enhances its performance on Bt-crops under field conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined laboratory and field data presented.

claim: Infection with HaDV2 was associated with significantly enhanced tolerance of cotton bollworm to HaNPV in laboratory trials.
source: Recently, we showed in laboratory trials that infection with a densovirus, Helicoverpa armigera densovirus-1 (HaDV2, named as HaDNV-1 previously, GenBank accession number: NC_015718), was associated with significantly enhanced tolerance of cotton bollworm, H. armigera, to a baculovirus (H. armigera nucleopolyhedrovirus, HaNPV) (Xu et al., 2014), and there was some suggestion that the densovirus also increased tolerance to Cry1Ac toxin in a Bt-susceptible strain of H. armigera (Xu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2017a; Xu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: There was some suggestion that HaDV2 increased tolerance to Cry1Ac toxin in a Bt-susceptible strain of H. armigera.
source: Recently, we showed in laboratory trials that infection with a densovirus, Helicoverpa armigera densovirus-1 (HaDV2, named as HaDNV-1 previously, GenBank accession number: NC_015718), was associated with significantly enhanced tolerance of cotton bollworm, H. armigera, to a baculovirus (H. armigera nucleopolyhedrovirus, HaNPV) (Xu et al., 2014), and there was some suggestion that the densovirus also increased tolerance to Cry1Ac toxin in a Bt-susceptible strain of H. armigera (Xu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2017a; Xu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: HaDV2 was mainly distributed in the fat body of the insect.

claim: HaDV2 infection in both Cry1Ac-resistant and Cry1Ac-susceptible strains of cotton bollworm enhances larval tolerance to Bt.
source: Laboratory experiments show that HaDV2 infection in both Cry1Ac-resistant and Cry1Ac-susceptible strains of cotton bollworm enhances larval tolerance to Bt and overall fitness.

source: Field experiments indicate that H. armigera populations infected with HaDV2 also have a higher tolerance to Bt-cotton relative to those not infected with HaDV2.
evidence: This is based on field experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The frequency of HaDV2-infected cotton bollworm is significantly higher in regions planted with Bt-cotton than in those areas where Bt-cotton is not grown.
source: Moreover, field monitoring over a 10-year period indicates that the frequency of HaDV2-infected cotton bollworm is significantly higher in regions planted with Bt-cotton than in those areas where Bt-cotton is not grown, and that in Bt-cotton-growing areas, the prevalence of HaDV2 infection increases with time since Bt-cotton adoption and with the proportion of cotton that is grown which is transgenic.
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data over 10 years.

claim: In Bt-cotton-growing areas, the prevalence of HaDV2 infection increases with time since Bt-cotton adoption.

claim: Increased Bt tolerance is associated with activated immune pathways to HaDV2 infection.

claim: Increased HaDV2 infection in cotton bollworm is correlated with the wide-scale adoption of Bt-cotton in China.
source: These results indicate that increased HaDV2 infection in cotton bollworm is correlated with the wide-scale adoption of Bt-cotton in China.
evidence: This is based on the combined field monitoring and experimental data.

claim: Two susceptible H. armigera strains infected with HaDV2 (96S and LF) both showed 1.5 times greater tolerance to Cry1Ac toxin relative to their corresponding non-infected controls.
source: Two susceptible H. armigera strains infected with HaDV2 (96S and LF) both showed 1.5 times greater tolerance to Cry1Ac toxin, relative to their corresponding non-infected controls (Supplementary file 1a and b).
evidence: This is based on bioassay data presented in supplementary files.

claim: In Cry1Ac-resistant strains (BtR, 96CAD, LFC2, LF5, LF60, LF120, and LF240), infection with HaDV2 showed a significant increase in their tolerance relative to the corresponding strains without HaDV2 infection, ranging between 30% and 130% enhanced tolerance.
source: In the case of the Cry1Ac-resistant strains (BtR, 96CAD, LFC2, LF5, LF60, LF120, and LF240), infection with HaDV2 again showed a significant increase in their tolerance relative to the corresponding strains without HaDV2 infection, ranging between 30% and 130% enhanced tolerance (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on bioassay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The slope of the regression line relating LC50 values of HaDV2-positive and HaDV2-negative strains is significantly greater than one.
source: The slope of the regression line is significantly greater than one (t-test: t=2.853, df=6, p=0.029), suggesting that the benefits of carrying HaDV2 may increase with increasing levels of Bt tolerance.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the bioassay data.

claim: The benefits of carrying HaDV2 may increase with increasing levels of Bt tolerance.
source: The slope of the regression line is significantly greater than one (t-test: t=2.853, df=6, p=0.029), suggesting that the benefits of carrying HaDV2 may increase with increasing levels of Bt tolerance.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis of the regression slope.

claim: For a given strain of H. armigera, larvae harboring HaDV2 were significantly more tolerant to Cry1Ac.
source: Logistic regression confirmed that for a given strain of H. armigera, larvae harboring HaDV2 were significantly more tolerant to Cry1Ac (GLM: Strain: χ28=36.57, p<0.0001, log10 (Cry1Ac toxin concentration): χ21=848.16, p<0.0001; Strain*log10(Cry1Ac toxin concentration): χ28=97.30, p<0.0001; HaDV2-status: χ21=9.53, p=0.0020).
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of bioassay data.

claim: There was no evidence that the benefits of hosting HaDV2 are affected by the tolerance level of the H. armigera strain.
source: However, there was no evidence that the benefits of hosting HaDV2 are affected by the tolerance level of the H. armigera strain, as reflected in the LC50 of the non-infected insects (χ21=0.06, p=0.80).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of bioassay data.

claim: At 8 days post-hatching, H. armigera larvae were significantly lighter when feeding on diet containing Bt than the ones without Bt.
source: At 8 days post-hatching, H. armigera larvae were significantly lighter (t=10.164, df=32, p<0.0001, n=17) and had lower HaDV2 viral loads in individuals feeding on diet containing Bt than the ones without Bt (t=4.527, df=32, p<0.0001, n=17), suggesting that Bt decreased the replication rate of HaDV2 by suppressing the growth of H. armigera larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 8 days post-hatching, H. armigera larvae had lower HaDV2 viral loads when feeding on diet containing Bt than the ones without Bt.
source: At 8 days post-hatching, H. armigera larvae were significantly lighter (t=10.164, df=32, p<0.0001, n=17) and had lower HaDV2 viral loads in individuals feeding on diet containing Bt than the ones without Bt (t=4.527, df=32, p<0.0001, n=17), suggesting that Bt decreased the replication rate of HaDV2 by suppressing the growth of H. armigera larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bt decreased the replication rate of HaDV2 by suppressing the growth of H. armigera larvae.

evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on larval weight and viral loads.

claim: Enhanced Bt-resistance in H. armigera LF, LF5, LF60, and LF240 strains was associated with lower larval survival rates.
source: Enhanced Bt-resistance in H. armigera LF, LF5, LF60, and LF240 strains was associated with lower larval survival rates, prolonged larval and pupal development (in both sexes), reduced pupal weight, lower adult emergence rate, and reduced fecundity and egg hatch rate; in contrast, sex ratio at emergence and the longevity of adults of both sexes were not influenced by the capacity to resist Cry1Ac toxin (Figure 2; Supplementary file 1c and d).
evidence: This is based on life-table data presented in Figure 2 and supplementary files.

claim: In the absence of HaDV2 infection, the fitness of the most Bt-resistant strain (LF240) was around 40% of that of the most Bt-susceptible strain (LF).
source: When traits were combined to estimate the fundamental net reproductive rates of the four H. armigera strains, R0 (Wang et al., 2016), this revealed that in the absence of HaDV2 infection, the fitness of the most Bt-resistant strain (LF240) was around 40% of that of the most Bt-susceptible strain (LF), consistent with a large fitness cost of resistance (Figure 3); strains with intermediate levels of resistance (LF5 and LF60) suffered a lower cost of resistance (c. 30% reduction in fitness).
evidence: This is based on R0 calculations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Strains with intermediate levels of resistance (LF5 and LF60) suffered a lower cost of resistance (c. 30% reduction in fitness).
source: When traits were combined to estimate the fundamental net reproductive rates of the four H. armigera strains, R0 (Wang et al., 2016), this revealed that in the absence of HaDV2 infection, the fitness of the most Bt-resistant strain (LF240) was around 40% of that of the most Bt-susceptible strain (LF), consistent with a large fitness cost of resistance (Figure 3); strains with intermediate levels of resistance (LF5 and LF60) suffered a lower cost of resistance (c. 30% reduction in fitness).
evidence: This is based on R0 calculations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Infection with HaDV2 rescued, or partially rescued, fitness loss in all four H. armigera strains showing a significant increase in R0 relative to their non-infected counterparts, averaging around 38% higher.
source: Infection with HaDV2 rescued, or partially rescued, this fitness loss, in all four H. armigera strains showing a significant increase in R0 relative to their non-infected counterparts, averaging around 38% higher (paired t-test: t=4.831, df=3, p=0.017; Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on R0 calculations and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: When infected with HaDV2, the R0 values of two of the three resistant strains (LF5 and LF60) were comparable to that of the non-infected susceptible (LF) strain.
source: Indeed, when infected with HaDV2, the R0 values of two of the three resistant strains (LF5 and LF60) were comparable to that of the non-infected susceptible (LF) strain (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on R0 calculations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Larval weight after 9 days growth was significantly affected by the cotton variety (Bt or non-Bt).
source: Larval weight after 9 days growth was significantly affected by the cotton variety (Bt or non-Bt) and by the HaDV2 infection-status (Supplementary file 1e and f), with larvae generally being heavier when fed with non-Bt-cotton than with Bt-cotton, and heavier for HaDV2-infected larvae than for larvae not infected with HaDV2; larvae were also heavier when they expressed lower levels of Bt-resistance, indicating that the cost of resistance is reflected in larval growth (Supplementary file 1e and f).
evidence: This is based on experimental data in supplementary files.

claim: Larval weight after 9 days growth was significantly affected by HaDV2 infection-status.
source: Larval weight after 9 days growth was significantly affected by the cotton variety (Bt or non-Bt) and by the HaDV2 infection-status (Supplementary file 1e and f), with larvae generally being heavier when fed with non-Bt-cotton than with Bt-cotton, and heavier for HaDV2-infected larvae than for larvae not infected with HaDV2; larvae were also heavier when they expressed lower levels of Bt-resistance, indicating that the cost of resistance is reflected in larval growth (Supplementary file 1e and f).

claim: None of the interactions between host plant, H. armigera strain, and infection-status explained any additional variation in larval weight.
source: None of the interactions between these three main effects explained any additional variation (model comparison with and without interaction terms: F=0.601, df=14, p=0.86), suggesting that the effects of host plant, H. armigera strain, and infection-status on larval growth were additive.
evidence: This is based on statistical model comparison.

claim: The effects of host plant, H. armigera strain, and infection-status on larval growth were additive.
source: None of the interactions between these three main effects explained any additional variation (model comparison with and without interaction terms: F=0.601, df=14, p=0.86), suggesting that the effects of host plant, H. armigera strain, and infection-status on larval growth were additive.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis.

claim: The prevalence of HaDV2 was extremely high (98% of 637 larvae in 2015; 97% of 180 larvae in 2016) in samples collected from Xiajin and Anci.
source: Across two successive years, the prevalence of HaDV2 was extremely high (98% of 637 larvae in 2015; 97% of 180 larvae in 2016).
evidence: This is based on field sampling data.

claim: The relative average development rates (RADRs) of individuals infected with HaDV2 were significantly higher than that of larvae not infected with the virus (0.62 vs. 0.52 in 2015; 0.61 vs. 0.53 in 2016).
source: Moreover, across both years, the relative average development rates (RADRs) (An et al., 2015) of individuals infected with HaDV2 were significantly higher than that of larvae not infected with the virus (0.62 vs. 0.52 in 2015; 0.61 vs. 0.53 in 2016) (linear model: infection status: F=28.80; df=1.815, p<0.0001; year: F=2.10, df=1.814, p=0.15; infection*year: F=0.57, df=1.813, p=0.57) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on field data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Over the 10-year period between 2007 and 2016, at both Xiajin and Anci provinces, HaDV2 infection rates increased significantly over time.
source: As predicted, over the 10-year period between 2007 and 2016, at both Xiajin and Anci provinces, HaDV2 infection rates increased significantly over time (logistic regression: Xiajin: χ21=405.79, p<0.0001; Anci: χ21=325.21, p<0.0001) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: There was a significant temporal increase in larval development rates (RADR) at both Xiajin and Anci locations.
source: Associated with this, there was a significant temporal increase in larval development rates (RADR) at both locations (linear models: Xiajin: F=5.474, df=1.8, p=0.047; Anci: F=23.256, df=1.8, p=0.0047) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Across the 10 years at both monitoring locations, there was a strong positive association between HaDV2 infection levels and RADRs.
source: Moreover, across the 10 years at both monitoring locations, there was a strong positive association between HaDV2 infection levels and RADRs, consistent with a possible causal relationship between these two temporal trends (linear models: Xiajin: F=23.826, df=1.9, P=0.001; Anci: F=13.676, df=1.9, P=0.006) (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Across all 3 years (2014-2016), HaDV2 infection levels in H. armigera were significantly higher at locations where Bt-cotton was planted (mean=82%) than in those where it was not (15%).
source: Across all 3 years, HaDV2 infection levels in H. armigera were significantly higher at locations where Bt-cotton was planted (mean=82%) than in those where it was not (15%) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (logistic regression: crop (Bt vs. non-Bt): χ21=354.15, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant year-by-crop interaction in HaDV2 infection levels.
source: There was also a significant year-by-crop interaction (χ21=24.13, p<0.0001) due to HaDV2 infection levels being uniformly high across the 3 years at sites growing Bt-cotton (81–90%), whereas infection levels gradually increased from 2014 to 2016 at non-Bt sites (12%, 16%, and 44%, respectively).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of field monitoring data.

claim: HaDV2 infection levels were uniformly high across the 3 years at sites growing Bt-cotton (81–90%).
source: There was also a significant year-by-crop interaction (χ21=24.13, p<0.0001) due to HaDV2 infection levels being uniformly high across the 3 years at sites growing Bt-cotton (81–90%), whereas infection levels gradually increased from 2014 to 2016 at non-Bt sites (12%, 16%, and 44%, respectively).
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data.

claim: Infection levels gradually increased from 2014 to 2016 at non-Bt sites (12%, 16%, and 44%, respectively).
source: There was also a significant year-by-crop interaction (χ21=24.13, p<0.0001) due to HaDV2 infection levels being uniformly high across the 3 years at sites growing Bt-cotton (81–90%), whereas infection levels gradually increased from 2014 to 2016 at non-Bt sites (12%, 16%, and 44%, respectively).
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data.

claim: Across the provinces where Bt-cotton is grown, the mean prevalence of HaDV2 in H. armigera between 2014 and 2016 increased with the number of years since Bt-cotton was first introduced.

claim: The mean prevalence of HaDV2 in H. armigera between 2014 and 2016 increased as the proportion of cotton that was transgenic increased.

claim: HaDV2 prevalence was not correlated with the proportional area of any of the other crops grown.

claim: Adding environmental variables to the minimal model did not significantly improve the model fit.

evidence: This is based on statistical model comparison.

claim: HaDV2 has a major effect on the gene expression profiles of their hosts.
source: Taken together with the hierarchical clustering of these DEGs, these results suggest that the HaDV2 has a major effect on the gene expression profiles of their hosts.

claim: Genes in ABC transporters pathway at 48 hr were significantly enriched and upregulated.

claim: There was a total of 1573 significant DEGs in HaDV2-negative insects after exposure to Cry1Ac (673 upregulated and 900 downregulated).

claim: Seven ABC transporter genes were differentially expressed (four upregulated and three downregulated) in HaDV2-negative insects after Cry1Ac exposure.
source: Seven ABC transporter genes, which are related to immunity, were differentially expressed (four upregulated and three downregulated) (Figure 9A); eight trypsin genes, which are related to the conversion of the protoxin to activated toxin, were differently expressed (six upregulated and two downregulated) (Figure 9B); two carboxylesterase genes, which are related to the detoxification of Bt by the insect, were upregulated; and two Bt toxin receptors genes, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and aminopeptidase N (APN), which are related to Bt resistance, were downregulated (Figure 9C).

source: One trypsin gene was downregulated; genes in the ascorbate and aldarate metabolism pathway, which is related to carbohydrate metabolism were upregulated; genes in drug metabolism – cytochrome P450 pathway, metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450 pathway and drug metabolism – and other enzymes pathways, which are related to detoxification, were also upregulated (Figure 9E).

claim: HaDV2 infection enhances tolerance to Cry1Ac in both susceptible and resistant strains of H. armigera.
source: Here, we show that HaDV2 infection enhances tolerance to Cry1Ac in both susceptible and resistant strains of H. armigera.
evidence: This is based on the bioassay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There appears to have been a strong positive selection for HaDV2-infected H. armigera in populations exposed to Cry1Ac-cotton in the field.
source: We also show that there appears to have been a strong positive selection for HaDV2-infected H. armigera in populations exposed to Cry1Ac-cotton in the field, especially (but not exclusively) when this exposure has been for prolonged periods of time.
evidence: This is based on field monitoring data showing increased prevalence over time.

claim: The temporal increase in RADR between 2002 and 2014 in Xiajin and Anci was ascribed to evolved genetic resistance to Cry1Ac in H. armigera in a previous study.
source: In a previous study of these two populations, the temporal increase in RADR between 2002 and 2014 was ascribed to evolved genetic resistance to Cry1Ac in H. armigera, despite the failure to identify the key genetic locus conferring resistance in these populations (An et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: The putative increase in genetic resistance over the period 2002-2014 may, at least in part, be due to the phenotypic expression of HaDV2 infection.
source: The relatively strong correlation between the annual prevalence of HaDV2 in H. armigera and their mean annual RADR in each of these populations (Figure 5E,F) suggests that the putative increase in genetic resistance over this period may, at least in part, be due to the phenotypic expression of HaDV2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: HaDV2-infected H. armigera not only accumulate more fat body than non-infected individuals, but they also grow faster and larger.
source: HaDV2-infected H. armigera not only accumulate more fat body than non-infected individuals, but they also grow faster and larger (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: Developmental resistance could provide a potential mechanism to explain the enhanced tolerance of densovirus-infected insects.
source: Therefore, developmental resistance could provide a potential mechanism to explain the enhanced tolerance of densovirus-infected insects.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism.

claim: HaDV2-infected larvae have more fat body than non-infected insects.
source: HaDV2-infected larvae have more fat body than non-infected insects (Xu et al., 2014), and the fat body plays an important role in insect immunity as it is a major site for the production and secretion of antimicrobial peptides (Hoffmann, 2003; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007), so immunological resistance is another potential mechanism by which HaDV2 may enhance resistance to both baculovirus and Cry1Ac.
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: The fat body plays an important role in insect immunity as it is a major site for the production and secretion of antimicrobial peptides.
source: HaDV2-infected larvae have more fat body than non-infected insects (Xu et al., 2014), and the fat body plays an important role in insect immunity as it is a major site for the production and secretion of antimicrobial peptides (Hoffmann, 2003; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007), so immunological resistance is another potential mechanism by which HaDV2 may enhance resistance to both baculovirus and Cry1Ac.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: Immunological resistance is a potential mechanism by which HaDV2 may enhance resistance to both baculovirus and Cry1Ac.
source: HaDV2-infected larvae have more fat body than non-infected insects (Xu et al., 2014), and the fat body plays an important role in insect immunity as it is a major site for the production and secretion of antimicrobial peptides (Hoffmann, 2003; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007), so immunological resistance is another potential mechanism by which HaDV2 may enhance resistance to both baculovirus and Cry1Ac.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism.

claim: In fruit flies and mosquitoes, the Jak-STAT pathway controls the expression of genes in response to infection with a range of viruses and bacteria.
source: In fruit flies and mosquitoes, this pathway controls the expression of genes in response to infection with a range of viruses and bacteria, including Drosophila C virus, dengue virus, West Nile virus, Escherichia coli, and Micrococcus luteus (Barillas-Mury et al., 1999; Marques and Imler, 2016).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: HaDV2 may not enhance resistance to Bt using traditional molecular resistance pathways.
source: We did not observe the differential expression of genes playing pivotal roles in Bt resistance of H. armigera, for example, cadherin, APN, and ALP (Chen et al., 2015; Gahan et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2009), suggesting that HaDV2 may not enhance resistance to Bt using traditional molecular resistance pathways, though we did observe that the ABC transporter pathways, which has been reported to be associated with Bt-resistance (Bretschneider et al., 2016; Dermauw and Van Leeuwen, 2014), were significantly upregulated at 48 hr post challenge.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA-seq data showing no differential expression of key resistance genes.

claim: The ABC transporter pathways were significantly upregulated at 48 hr post challenge.
source: We did not observe the differential expression of genes playing pivotal roles in Bt resistance of H. armigera, for example, cadherin, APN, and ALP (Chen et al., 2015; Gahan et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2009), suggesting that HaDV2 may not enhance resistance to Bt using traditional molecular resistance pathways, though we did observe that the ABC transporter pathways, which has been reported to be associated with Bt-resistance (Bretschneider et al., 2016; Dermauw and Van Leeuwen, 2014), were significantly upregulated at 48 hr post challenge.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The mode of action of Bt toxins agrees that Bt protoxins are first converted to activated toxins by midgut proteases.
source: Generally, the mode of action of Bt toxins agrees that Bt protoxins are first converted to activated toxins by midgut proteases, then the toxins bind to the midgut receptors, for example, CAD, APN, and ALP, finally leading to insect death (Xiao and Wu, 2019).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: In insects lacking HaDV2, Cry1Ac increased the activation of Bt protoxins by increasing the expression level of proteases, such as trypsin.
source: In insects lacking HaDV2, Cry1Ac increased the activation of Bt protoxins by increasing the expression level of proteases, such as trypsin.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: In a defensive response to Cry1Ac, receptor genes of H. armigera, such as APN and ALP, were significantly downregulated to reduce the toxin-binding capacity.
source: In a defensive response to Cry1Ac, receptor genes of H. armigera, such as APN and ALP, were significantly downregulated to reduce the toxin-binding capacity.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and represents an inference about the biological function.

claim: Carboxylesterase genes and most of ABC transporters genes were significantly upregulated to improve insect immunity in response to Cry1Ac.
source: Carboxylesterase genes and most of ABC transporters genes were significantly upregulated to improve insect immunity, while other pathways related to antimicrobials, for example, MAPK signaling pathways, were significantly downregulated, reducing resistance to Bt toxin (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Other pathways related to antimicrobials, for example, MAPK signaling pathways, were significantly downregulated, reducing resistance to Bt toxin.
source: Carboxylesterase genes and most of ABC transporters genes were significantly upregulated to improve insect immunity, while other pathways related to antimicrobials, for example, MAPK signaling pathways, were significantly downregulated, reducing resistance to Bt toxin (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: When H. armigera larvae were infected with HaDV2, genes and pathways related to Bt response were generally not significantly enriched after Cry1Ac exposure.
source: In contrast, when H. armigera larvae were infected with HaDV2, these genes and pathways were generally not significantly enriched after Cry1Ac exposure: one trypsin gene was downregulated and some genes involved in drug metabolism were upregulated to increase the metabolism of xenobiotics, improving Bt tolerance.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Some genes involved in drug metabolism were upregulated to increase the metabolism of xenobiotics, improving Bt tolerance in HaDV2-infected larvae.
source: In contrast, when H. armigera larvae were infected with HaDV2, these genes and pathways were generally not significantly enriched after Cry1Ac exposure: one trypsin gene was downregulated and some genes involved in drug metabolism were upregulated to increase the metabolism of xenobiotics, improving Bt tolerance.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and represents an inference about the biological function.

claim: The data support the notion that HaDV2 increased the Bt tolerance level of H. armigera via related immune mechanisms.
source: In spite of this, our data still support the notion that HaDV2 increased the Bt tolerance level of H. armigera via related immune mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for the observations is that HaDV2 directly or indirectly enhances tolerance of H. armigera to Bt in the field.
source: Whilst data from the field are inevitably correlational, when combined with the laboratory experiments, we feel that the most parsimonious explanation for the observations reported here is that HaDV2 directly or indirectly enhances tolerance of H. armigera to Bt in the field, probably via increasing larval growth rates and via priming of immune defenses.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined laboratory and field data.

claim: HaDV2 probably enhances tolerance of H. armigera to Bt via increasing larval growth rates and via priming of immune defenses.
source: Whilst data from the field are inevitably correlational, when combined with the laboratory experiments, we feel that the most parsimonious explanation for the observations reported here is that HaDV2 directly or indirectly enhances tolerance of H. armigera to Bt in the field, probably via increasing larval growth rates and via priming of immune defenses.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined laboratory and field data.

claim: It is not feasible to manipulate HaDV2 infection status in the field in order to enhance the capacity of Bt to manage H. armigera because of the lack of suitable antivirals and because of the efficient vertical and horizontal transmission of this virus in the field.
source: Although we show that HaDV2 increases the tolerance of its host to Bt, it is not feasible to manipulate HaDV2 infection status in the field in order to enhance the capacity of Bt to manage H. armigera because of the lack of suitable antivirals (against HaDV2) and because of the efficient vertical and horizontal transmission of this virius in the field.
evidence: This is a practical inference about the feasibility of field manipulation.
